papers.title: A Compact Statistical View of Musical-Instrument Directivity
papers.abstract: Directivity is a defining feature of musical-instrument radiation and is known to vary strongly with frequency. With the growing availability of measured directivity datasets and their use in sound-field simulation and spatial audio, there is a practical need for representations that are both compact and comparable across sources. This work addresses that need by proposing a statistically grounded description of frequency-dependent directivity that reduces complex radiation patterns to a small set of meaningful descriptors. The approach enables directivity patterns to be summarized in an interpretable way and compared consistently across frequency bands, even when the radiation is not well described by a single dominant direction. The resulting representation supports tasks such as analysis, categorization, and model building, providing a bridge between detailed measurements and higher-level descriptors useful for musical acoustics and audio rendering. Experiments on a corpus of 41 orchestral instruments show that the proposed method preserves the distance geometry well while reducing the full order-4, 30-band corpus from about 492~kB to about 100~kB in double-precision storage.

papers.title: Semi-analytical representation of the Gaunt-modified Landau-Lifshitz equation in a plane wave
papers.abstract: We analyze electron dynamics in a plane electromagnetic wave using the Landau-Lifshitz equation with a quantum radiation reaction correction modelled by a Gaunt factor. In this geometry, the quantum parameter $\chi$ depends solely on the lightfront momentum, allowing the modified equation of motion to retain the integrable structure of the classical problem. We derive a semi-analytical solution for the energy evolution and the four-velocity, which reduces to the known classical result in the appropriate limit. The results provide an analytical and deterministic description of semiclassical radiation reaction in plane-wave fields.

papers.title: From Rock Tumbling to Telescope Mirror Grinding: How Optical Perfection Emerges from Random Motion
papers.abstract: When two glass disks are rubbed together by hand with an abrasive between them, their surfaces spontaneously converge to perfectly matching spherical curves, accurate to tens of nanometers. How does such optical precision emerge from an essentially random manual process? Starting from Preston's law of material removal, we derive a first-principles explanation. Symmetries of the grinding stroke imply that planes and spheres are the generic equilibria of the process. Their stability is governed by a hierarchy of timescales: small-scale irregularities decay exponentially on the grinding timescale $T_\text{grind}$, while large-scale deviations from a sphere diffuse away on the longer spherizing timescale $T_\text{sphere} \propto (R_\text{mirror}/R_\text{stroke})^2\, T_\text{grind}$. Gravity and finite disk size destabilize planar surfaces, but for sufficiently short strokes spheres remain stable ($T_\text{deform} \gg T_\text{sphere}$), with only their radius of curvature varying adiabatically. The same framework unifies telescope mirror grinding with everyday phenomena: rock tumbling (explaining why rotary tumbling rounds edges more than vibratory, and why neither produce spheres) and sanding (explaining why small flat surfaces inevitably round). These examples offer an accessible classroom context for stable and unstable equilibria, exponential relaxation, diffusion, multi-timescale analysis, and the emergence of the Laplacian operator from averaging over a local area.

papers.title: Which Adiabatic Cycles Alter an Action Variable?
papers.abstract: Action variables are adiabatic invariants: their values are preserved during adiabatic time evolutions in completely integrable classical Hamiltonian systems. Nevertheless, an adiabatic cycle can alter how an action variable depends on phase-space variables that are independent of adiabatic parameters. Such a change, which we call action variable holonomy, induces adiabatic torus pumping in phase space. For a family of completely integrable kicked-top systems, a homotopy classification of adiabatic cycles identifies which adiabatic cycles induce action variable holonomy and adiabatic torus pumping. A physical example is also provided.

papers.title: Spin-induced lateral acoustic forces on chiral and achiral particles
papers.abstract: Acoustic spin enables intriguing chiral sound-matter interactions, yet its mechanical consequences remain much less explored. Here, we demonstrate spin-induced lateral acoustic forces on chiral and achiral particles coupled to a substrate. Under plane-wave incidence, left- and right-handed chiral particles scatter fields with opposite acoustic spin that selectively couple to counterpropagating guided waves, generating lateral forces of opposite signs on the enantiomers. The lateral forces can also be realized for achiral particles by employing acoustic vortex-beam illumination. We experimentally validate the spin-dependent excitation of guided waves and lateral forces. Our results provide a route to spin-controlled acoustic manipulation and chirality-selective particle transport.

papers.title: Quantifying Bicycle Setup Differences on the Road: Field Estimates of CdA, Crr and Power Demand
papers.abstract: Individual bicycle configurations can be assessed in situ using power and speed measurements without a velodrome or wind tunnel. We apply an integrated energy-balance workflow to five configurations tested by one rider on a road section. Five nominal power levels, each ridden in both directions, yield 25 paired observations. Kinetic-energy changes are corrected explicitly; gravitational work cancels between spatially matched outward and return sections. A shared effective rolling-resistance coefficient Crr and a separate aerodynamic drag area CdA for each setup are estimated jointly. The fitted drag areas range from 0.2288 to 0.3601m^2, with a common Crr=0.00551 +/- 0.00047. At 40km/h, the estimated differences are 17.4 +/- 5.5W favouring the EZ-covered over the uncovered 80mm rear-wheel configuration and 64.3 +/- 4.0W favouring the aerobar position over the drops on the tested road bike. The helmet swap yields a difference of 3.5 +/- 2.8W. Reported uncertainties combine statistical variability and assumed input uncertainties and represent one standard deviation. The study demonstrates a practical workflow for quantifying individual setup differences and connecting resistance estimates to power-speed predictions under specified reference conditions.

papers.title: A new perspective in linear Cauchy Elasticity: variational minimum principles for statics, dynamics, and heterogeneous materials
papers.abstract: A variational minimum principle for linear elastodynamics of a possibly heterogeneous material without a stored energy function is developed. It involves a change of variables to dual fields, and results in a degenerate elliptic Euler-Lagrange system, even when the primal elastodynamics is hyperbolic. Uniqueness assertions for the dual dynamic and static problems and implications of the degenerate ellipticity are sketched. Some implications pertaining to heterogeneous materials and ones with indefinite elastic moduli are discussed.

papers.title: Newtonian and Relativistic Particle Mechanics from Local Energy Conservation: A Symmetry-Selected Force-Energy Framework
papers.abstract: We develop a formulation of particle mechanics in which the functional relation between force and kinetic energy is derived directly from the instantaneous (pointwise along the trajectory) conservation of mechanical energy $E$, rather than postulated through Newton's second law or a variational principle. Starting from the condition $\dot{E}=0$, we derive a generalized force law that does not assume a specific kinetic-energy function, momentum-velocity relation, or equation of motion. The resulting inertial response naturally decomposes into a component parallel to the acceleration, responsible for changes in kinetic energy, and a transverse component that preserves energy while altering the direction of motion. Imposing rotational equivariance constrains the geometric structure of the force law, while the relativity principle between inertial reference frames further restricts its admissible realizations. In strictly one-dimensional motion, inertial frame equivalence, supplemented by a set of five structural properties, implies invariance of the total force under inertial boosts; together with local energy conservation, this uniquely fixes the functional form of kinetic energy and momentum. Galilean invariance selects the Newtonian expressions, whereas Lorentz invariance yields the relativistic ones. The framework unifies conservative and non-conservative (yet non-dissipative, e.g., the magnetic Lorentz force) dynamics at the single-particle level and clarifies the precise conditions under which energy-based and variational formulations of mechanics are dynamically equivalent. Newtonian and relativistic mechanics thus emerge as symmetry-selected realizations of a common energy-conserving force-energy structure. The analysis further shows that the standard Lagrangian form $L=T-V$ is consistent with, and implicitly presupposes, Galilean relativity.

papers.title: From Symmetry and Continuity to the Lorentz Transformation
papers.abstract: We derive the Lorentz transformation from spacetime symmetries and continuity, without assuming the invariance of the speed of light. Spacetime homogeneity yields an additive coordinate map; continuity along four linearly independent inertial worldlines, together with additivity, establishes linearity throughout spacetime. Spatial isotropy and the assumed continuous local one-parameter group structure of collinear boosts yield velocity reciprocity and determine a generalized Lorentz-type family parameterized by $\kappa$. The velocity law and the empirical identification of its invariant speed with the coordinate speed of light in vacuum select the Lorentzian branch, fixing $\kappa=-1/c^2$ and recovering the Lorentz transformation.

papers.title: Generalization of Rayleigh's high-frequency theory for the 2D Helmholtz equation in a half-space subject to a radiation condition at infinity and a Dirichlet condition on a 1D periodically-uneven boundary
papers.abstract: The 2D Helmholtz equation, radiation condition and Dirichlet boundary condition, are the translation, in mathematical terms, of (at least) three physical 2D problems for the prediction of the total scalar wavefield on one side of an impenetrable 1D periodically uneven boundary when: a) a plane TE electromagnetic wave propagating in the vacuum strikes the boundary the other side of which is occupied by a perfectly-conducting medium, b) a plane SH elastic elastic wave strikes a rigid boundary, c) a plane acoustic wave strikes a pressure-release boundary. The first attempt to solve such problems in a non-heuristic manner was made by Lord Rayleigh (in his book, 'The Theory of Sound' which appeared in 1896). My task will be to revisit Rayleigh's theory of diffraction by a sinusoidal-shaped, impenetrable boundary, and more specifically, his perturbation method for obtaining a mathematically-explicit solution to the diffraction problem in the high-frequency regime. In so doing, I shall correct and generalize Rayleigh's method to obtain solutions for arbitrary angles of incidence as well as for 1D periodic impenetrable boundaries of quite-general shape.

papers.title: Free Precession Revisited: A Vector-Only Analysis of Gyroscopic Dynamic Equilibrium
papers.abstract: This paper presents a self-contained, vector-only formulation of gyroscope precession about a fixed pivot -- gravity-driven, not the torque-free Euler-Poinsot case. The derivation of its governing equation uses vector integrals and cross products of intrinsic vectors, with no component decomposition; no tensor or dyadic formalism, matrix or Euler angle enters. Inertia about the center of mass enters through two mass integrals alone: the polar second moment of mass $J_0$ (isotropic) and the vector operator $\vec F$ (the rest, including all non-isotropic inertia). Using material time derivatives referenced to the inertial observer, the torque about the pivot is assembled once from the complete acceleration of each mass element, giving an exact, unified vector equation for steady precession. The balance of the gravity torque against this inertia torque reproduces the classical steady-precession relation of the heavy symmetric top exactly at non-vertical tilts, on both the slow and fast branches, with the horizontal-shaft case exact rather than approximate. Closed forms are given for the disk, sphere, and circular and rectangular toruses. The constant tilt angle of dynamic equilibrium is explained as torque equalization: the two torques about the pivot balance exactly at that tilt and unequally on either side of it, treated throughout as a geometric function of the tilt under constant precession and self-spin rates, and never as a function of time. Informationally equivalent to the classical description, the work contributes, in order, an interpretation (the classical balance read in torque vectors throughout) and the vector method as its tool. The exact relation predates this work: Klein and Sommerfeld stated it in 1897, Brand in 1930. Begun by the author in 1975 and re-verified symbolically, the work is intended for undergraduate readers, with every step of the derivation stated.

papers.title: Statistical foundations of revised reverberation theory for a diffuse sound field in a room
papers.abstract: Revised reverberation theory is reformulated statistically for a diffuse sound field to clarify how the mean residual free path connects direct sound, reflected sound, and room energy decay. Under completely absorptive conditions, direct sound persists until reaching a boundary, producing decay after the source stops even without reflections. An integral-geometric relation connects the mean residual free path to the second moment of the wall-to-wall free path, thereby linking the mean propagation distance of direct sound to the temporal variance of reflected sound under an independent-renewal approximation. Using this relationship, the macroscopic decay rate and the microscopic long-time asymptotic decay rate agree exactly through second order in the absorption coefficient under an independent-renewal approximation. A gamma model with a consistent residual free-path distribution eliminates probability at negative arrival times. Ray-tracing simulations in three rectangular rooms support the predicted initial decay slopes under completely absorptive conditions and reverberation predictions for absorption coefficients up to 0.5. Engineering approximations yield macroscopic formulas requiring only room volume, surface area, and absorption coefficient while reducing prediction errors relative to the Sabine and Eyring formulas. A supplementary fixed-source and local-receiver test supports T30 prediction within the tested conditions. These results establish a common statistical basis for direct and reflected sound and connect the physical interpretation of reverberation to practical prediction.
